claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The nanoparticles are initially crystallized as a solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by competition between entropic solid-solution stabilization and enthalpic driving forces for phase separation or ordering.
Temperature variation from 473 to 1923 K affects nanoparticle stability.
Short-range order and lattice distortion mediate the response to temperature.
The nanoparticles will maintain structural and chemical stability across the operating-temperature range.
Deviations from stability may occur at high temperatures.
High-temperature deviations would arise from increased enthalpic driving forces.
The initial low-temperature solid solution is the baseline for comparison.
In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy can measure lattice parameters, phase composition, and chemical ordering.
Significant phase separation or ordering below 1273 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The outcome predicts maintenance of stability across the full 473–1923 K range while simultaneously allowing deviations at high temperatures within that same range, so the prediction is not unambiguously defined.
